doc.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Starting trombone, violin and other lessons
summary: At about eight he picks the trombone off a music store wall, studies with neighbour Mr. Mayhall, and also takes piano, tap dance and voice lessons.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Was there a point where you decided, in your teens perhaps, that you were going to be a musician?

Not professionally. I really hadn’t made up my mind that that was the particular direction I was going to go in after my schooling. But I definitely was quite interested. Well I was probably about eight years old when I was — well two doors down the street from where I lived was a trombone player. And he played in the old days in vaudeville theatres. He used to play for the vaudeville acts in the little pit orchestra. So well I’d already started on the violin. So my mother and father were acquainted with Mr. Paul Morrison. He was the instructor at the local Quincy High School. And he said to my mother and father, you know, “It’s nice that Bob is playing the violin, but why don’t we see if we can get him a © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

brass instrument also. Maybe we could work him in to the marching band when he gets older.” So they took me down to the music store and at that point I didn’t know what instrument I might want to play. So they had all these instruments on the wall, just sort of hanging there, and they said, “Look up there and pick out an instrument that you think you might like to learn.” And I didn’t know really one from another basically, so I just happened to point to the trombone. Well it was fortunate that just very close to where we lived was a trombone player, Mr. Mayhall. So they had a convenient instructor there. So Mr. Mayhall started giving me lessons. I was about eight years old. And I guess I was somewhat a slow learner at that time, about certain things. Maybe not about the music, but my teacher said, “You know I think you’re going to learn to play the horn before you learn how to put it in the case.” Because I never could remember how to get it in the case.
No kidding. How to take it apart?
How to take it apart and get it the right side up.
You’re lucky you didn’t play the bassoon or something like that, you never would have got it in.

But I took formal lessons maybe three or four years on the trombone. And also I might add that I also started on piano, because we had a piano at home. And my mother knew another piano player that was a good teacher. So she started me out on the piano and the trombone, practically at the same time. And so I just started showing various talents in different directions you know, and also I ended up taking tap dance lessons.
And at one time I was taking violin lessons, trombone lessons, tap dance lessons, and some voice lessons. So I was getting a little bit of everything.
Would you like to show us a little of your tap dance routine?
I don’t think so. I think I know maybe two steps and that’s about all I can remember.
